topic: plan: Airy to Challis, 9 July 1846 (No. 15)
quotation: You know that I attach importance to the examination of that part of the heavens in which there is * * * * reason for suspecting the existence of a planet exterior to Uranus. I have thought about the way of making such examination, but I am convinced that (for various reasons, of declination, latitude of place, feebleness of light, and regularity of superintendence) there is no prospect whatever of its being made with any chance of success, except with the Northumberland Telescope. Now I should be glad to ask you, in the first place, whether you could make such an examination? Presuming that your answer would be in the negative, I would ask, secondly, whether, supposing that an assistant were supplied to you for this purpose, you would superintend the examination? You will readily perceive that all this is in a most unformed state at present, and that I am asking these questions almost at a venture, in the hope of rescuing the matter from a state which is, without the assistance that you and your instruments can give, almost desperate. Therefore I should be glad to have your answer, not only responding simply to my questions, but also entering into any other considerations which you think likely to bear on the matter. The time for the said examination is approaching near.
notes: Airy's gloss follows: he thought the planet visible only in large telescopes and was prepared to supply an efficient assistant

topic: plan: the Suggestions transmitted 13 July (No. 16)
quotation: On the 13th of July, I transmitted to Professor Challis "Suggestions for the Examination of a Portion of the Heavens in search of the external Planet which is presumed to exist and to produce disturbance in the motion of Uranus," and I accompanied them with the following letter:— [No. 16. G. B. Airy to Professor Challis. Royal Observatory, Greenwich, 1846, July 13.] I have drawn up the enclosed paper, in order to give you a notion of the extent of work incidental to a sweep for the possible planet. I only add at present that, in my opinion, the importance of this inquiry exceeds that of any current work, which is of such a nature as not to be totally lost by delay.

topic: modification: star density in 9′ zones, stars allowed to pass
quotation: By taking stars of that order of magnitude, I found that, although the breadth of each zone was not more than 9′, they came in such quick succession that in dark nights there was seldom any intermission in setting down the observations. It was often the case, when the stars came in groups, that some were necessarily allowed to pass without recording their places. It also not unfrequently happened, when even the stars were more scattered, that several, of a degree of brightness which it was desirable not to let pass, had nearly the same right ascension; and in such instances it was either not possible to take them all, or, if the attempt were made, in the hurry of observing there was great chance of making mistakes.

topic: modification: supplementary mode adopted
quotation: To obviate these inconveniences, and to make the search more complete, I adopted a supplementary mode of observing, which was suggested by a particular arrangement in the apparatus of the Northumberland equatoreal, and which, as it differs in principle from the methods usually employed in mapping stars, I will describe more particularly.

topic: modification: definition of the two methods
quotation: In the former of the two methods of observing adverted to above, the telescope was perfectly stationary, moving neither in hour-angle nor declination. In the other, the telescope, with polar frame and hour-circle, was carried by clock-movement nearly at the rate of sidereal time, but was not moved in declination. I shall distinguish the two methods by saying "telescope fixed" and "telescope moving."

topic: modification: assistant with telescope fixed
quotation: When the telescope was fixed, I had one assistant to aid in recording the observations. He sat at a table with the memorandum-book and chronometer before him, and his part was to begin counting from the chronometer on a signal being given, and to write down the time of transit, declination reading, and magnitude of the star, as I gave them out, together with such occasional remarks as the observations seemed to require.

topic: modification: telescope moving, tangent screw and two assistants
quotation: The method of observing with the telescope moving was conducted by means of a tangent screw attached to the polar frame, and a handle extending to the observer's seat, which enabled him to move the polar frame and telescope relatively to the hour-circle, while the hour-circle, polar frame, and telescope, were carried by the clock-movement. It is clear that in this way the stars might be brought up at leisure to the toothed border of the comb at which the bisections were made, without the risk of any star passing which it was thought desirable to take. This method, however, required reading off the hour-circle, by which, in fact, differences of right ascension were measured; and to carry on the observations with convenience and rapidity, it was necessary to have the help of my two assistants, Mr. MORGAN and Mr. BREEN. Mr. MORGAN noted down, on a signal, first, the chronometer time of bisection (which was not required with much accuracy), then the declination reading and magnitude of the star, as I gave them out, and, lastly, the hour-circle reading given by Mr. BREEN. Instead of bisecting the divisions of the hour-circle, it was more convenient to bisect the divisions of a small graduated arc, which I had the means of clamping to the hour-circle, the intervals between its divisions being well ascertained. The chronometer times were required for correcting differences of right ascension measured by the hour-circle for the hour-circle's rate.
other_values: assistants Mr. Morgan and Mr. Breen
notes: continues on p. 419 (memoirs16_p454.png)

topic: modification: eye at eye-piece; recording without cessation
quotation: It will appear that in each of these methods the observer's eye was not required to quit the eye-piece, and that in the second method the recording of the observations could go on without cessation, however the stars were grouped.

topic: modification: result of trial of the two methods
quotation: On making trial of these methods, I found that with the telescope moving I took more stars in the same portion of the heavens than with the telescope fixed, but that fewer stars were taken in the same time; so that the former method occupied a considerably longer time in sweeping over a given portion of the heavens than the latter, but swept more completely.

topic: modification: plan of first sweep fixed, then moving
quotation: Finding this to be the case, and taking into account also the interruptions caused by winding up the clock and adjusting the tangent-screw when it had gone to its limit, I determined to proceed as follows: first, to go over the tract proposed to be scrutinised, or a portion of it at a time, with telescope fixed, taking as many stars as could be conveniently taken without risk of mistakes from too much haste, and then to go over the same portion with telescope moving. In this way there would be no chance of error from irregularities or interruptions in the going of the clock, as the first sweep would always furnish a sufficient number of points of reference for determining the clock's rate at any time for the second sweep.

topic: modification: second sweep to include all stars of first; third sweep if needed
depth_magnitude: stars to the 11th magnitude, and all brighter
quotation: Also, as the second sweep might be expected to include all the stars contained in the first, the probability was that the object for which the observations were undertaken would be attained by the second sweep, without the necessity of a third. If, however, it turned out otherwise, I intended to go over the tract a third time; and, if this scrutiny proved unsuccessful, I should only have had the satisfaction of mapping a certain portion of the heavens so as to include stars to the 11th magnitude, and all brighter, in a more perfect manner than in any previous undertaking of a similar kind.

topic: modification: clouds with telescope fixed
quotation: When it happened (as it often did happen) that a cloud came over and obscured the field of view, I immediately left my seat, if the telescope at the time were fixed, and set the clock going, directing at the same time my assistant to draw a line separating the observations before such an occurrence from those that followed. On resuming the observations after the cloud removed, the star last taken before the interruption was the first of the new series.

topic: modification: clouds with telescope moving

topic: modification: reference stars and the 80′ sector
zone_dec: movable in north polar distance through 80′
quotation: For the purpose of determining precisely the positions of the zones, stars of reference were taken in each series. To explain how this was done, it is necessary to state that the Northumberland equatoreal has no declination circle, the setting of the telescope in north polar distance being effected by graduated rods. The rod remaining in position, the telescope, by an arrangement proper for the purpose, is movable in north polar distance through 80′, and arcs to that extent may be measured by means of a graduated sector arc and microscope micrometer. When, therefore, on looking into the finder, a star was seen within reach of the sector, and bright enough to be likely to be in standard catalogues, by turning the sector milled head it was brought into the field of view of the large telescope; it was then accurately bisected by a fixed micrometer wire, a transit of it was taken, and the sector microscope micrometer was read off. The telescope was afterwards accurately restored to its former position by means of the sector-arc and its microscope micrometer. The readings of the hour-circle and declination rod being noted, and the error of the chronometer ascertained by comparison with the transit clock, it was easy to identify the reference star.

topic: modification: the one occasion observed entirely by the sector
quotation: On one occasion the observations were entirely conducted in the manner just stated, the telescope being moved in declination upwards and downwards through 80′, while the instrument was motionless about the polar axis. In this instance brighter stars only were selected, being intended as points of reference for the observations in narrow zones.

topic: modification: why a second mode; the instrument
quotation: But as such stars are very numerous, and frequently would have interfered with each other, another mode of observing was sometimes followed, which can only be successfully practised with an instrument of a similar construction with that employed. The Northumberland equatoreal has, at its lower end, a complete hour circle, divided to 24 hours and moved uniformly by clockwork. This circle is wholly detached from the frame of the equatoreal, turning freely on the lower pivot, but the two can be attached at pleasure, when their relative positions can be altered at the will of the observer by a tangent screw, and measured by vernier readings or microscopes. If the hour circle and the clock be properly adjusted, the apparent right ascension of any object is read off at once upon the circle; and the error, either of the hour circle or clock, can be ascertained and eliminated by the observation of known stars.

topic: modification: telescope moving, assistants
quotation: By the handle which governs the tangent screw, the observer is enabled to bring each star in order of right ascension to the meridian wire, and to give out the relative declination, magnitude, &c. to one assistant, who writes this down with the corresponding time by chronometer, while a second assistant reads off the apparent right ascension on the hour circle. The known stars thus observed furnish the correction of the declination wire, of the hour circle, and of the rate. Professor Challis distinguishes this from the ordinary method by the words "telescope moving."

topic: modification: trial result and plan of first ordinary then moving
quotation: On making trial of both methods, it was found that more stars were noted in the same space, but fewer stars in the same time when the observations were made "telescope moving." Hence, the Professor determined to go over the required space as carefully as possible, first in the ordinary method, and then a second time with the "telescope moving;" if the planet were not then discovered by its motion, it would, most probably, be found among the stars of the second operation which were not found in the first.

I found accordingly, in the library of the University of Cambridge, hour xxii., which extends over a small part of the space intended to be scrutinised; but I did not find hour xxi., and consequently concluded that it was not published.

quotation: The general accordance of M. LE VERRIER's results respecting the mass and orbit of the unknown planet with those of Mr. ADAMS, previously known to me, inspired renewed confidence in the theoretical deductions, and induced me to alter my plan of operations. On the evening of September 29, I swept over a considerable breadth in declination, within the limits of longitude marked out by M. LE VERRIER, resolving, if possible, to include the planet. The night was a good one; I observed without intermission three hours and a half, and recorded the positions of nearly 300 stars, paying more particular attention to the physical appearance of the brighter stars. topic: the comparison to No. 39 and No. 49; cloud at No. 39

quotation: On examining my early observations, I had the great vexation of finding that, if I had completed the comparison of the observations of July 30 and August 12, I should have discovered the planet, and spared myself all further labour. In the first examination, I found that every star, to No. 39 of the series taken on August 12 with telescope fixed, was in the series taken on July 30 with telescope moving. If I had gone on to No. 49, I should have found that a star of the 8th magnitude was wanting in the latter series. According to the principle of the search, this could be nothing less than a planet: it had wandered into the zone in the interval between July 30 and August 12. The only reason I can now give for not carrying the comparison further is, that the observations were interrupted at No. 39 by a cloud, the clock was set going, and a line of separation drawn in the memorandum-book. I proceeded to this line and no further.

To be quite sure of this second position, I have since directed the telescope to that point of the heavens, and found that no star is now to be seen there.

quotation: From the foregoing narrative it will appear, that it only required proceeding a little way in mapping the recorded positions of the stars to detect the planet. I delayed doing this, partly from being occupied with comet reductions, and partly from the fixed impression I had, that a long search was required to insure success.

topic: stated errors of the positions; 75 Aquarii check
quotation: The errors of right ascension are probably not greater than those incidental to determinations by single transits. From estimations already made, the error of north polar distance in the mean of the results by all the stars of comparison, may amount to 3″ on Aug. 4, and to 4″ on Aug. 12. It should be mentioned that, on the latter day, the parts of the micrometer revolution in the observation of the planet were estimated to a tenth, and not, as in general, to a fourth, implying more than usual care in taking the observation. To give an idea of the weight to be attached to the place of Aug. 12, I calculated the right ascension and north polar distance of 75 Aquarii by the same process as that by which the planet's place was obtained, and compared the results with the right ascension and north polar distance of the British Association Catalogue. The difference of right ascension was 0s·23, and that of north polar distance 3″·43.

Mr. Adams had found the mass to be about three times that of Uranus, and had thence inferred that the brightness would not be below that of a star of the ninth magnitude. He had mentioned this to Professor Challis, who preferred, nevertheless, proceeding on his original plan, as less liable to ultimate disappointment.

Le Verrier's results respecting the mass and orbit of the unseen planet with those of Mr. Adams, as it gave greater confidence, induced Professor Challis again to modify his mode of observing. The evening of Sept. 29 was favourable, and a considerable breadth in declination was swept over within the limits of longitude pointed out by M. Le Verrier, paying particular attention to the physical appearance of the brighter stars, in accordance with his suggestion. Out of the 300 stars thus observed, only one attracted particular attention, and to this the assistant was directed to add the note, "It seems to have a disk."

topic: the comparison to No. 39 and No. 49; cloud

comparison: stars up to No. 39 of August 12 all found in July 30; No. 49 in the former series wanting in the latter
quotation: On looking back at his earlier observations, Professor Challis had the vexation of finding that if he had compared all the observations of July 30 and August 12, the planet would then have been detected. The stars up to No. 39 of the series of August 12, "telescope fixed," were all found in the series taken July 30, "telescope moving." If this comparison had gone on a little further, it would have been found that No. 49 in the former series, a star of the eighth magnitude, was wanting in the latter series. From the principle of the search this must have been a planet. (It had, in fact, wandered into the zone between July 30 and August 12.) The comparison was really undertaken for another purpose, and probably was discontinued at that time after No. 39, as a cloud then interrupted the observations, after which a line of separation was drawn in the memorandum-book, and the clock was set going.

topic: letter: Challis to Airy, 18 July 1846 (No. 17, extracts)
quotation: I have only just returned from my excursion. * * * I have determined on sweeping for this hypothetical planet. * * * With respect to your proposal of supplying an assistant I need not say any thing, as I understand it to be made on the supposition that I decline undertaking the search myself. * * * I purpose to carry the sweep to the extent you recommend.
